endorsements.quote: Nurses are well placed to work directly with MDWs and community health workers in co‐designing digital health tools that genuinely reflect user needs (Greenhalgh et al. 2017 ).

Third, equity‐focused analyses must disaggregate findings by language, nationality, education, and employment conditions to detect differential impacts and avoid one‐size‐fits‐all conclusions (Lorenc et al. 2013 ).

Bias assessments are equally important: AI tools trained primarily on English‐language data and Western healthcare contexts may perform poorly for MDWs from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds (Obermeyer et al. 2019 ).

Evaluation protocols should therefore include regular accuracy audits benchmarking AI outputs against validated clinical guidelines, systematic tracking of error patterns, and user comprehension checks to see whether MDWs can distinguish reliable from unreliable information (World Health Organization 2023 ).

In practice, this might involve establishing validation routines that check AI outputs against evidence‐based guidelines, creating escalation pathways so complex questions reach human clinicians, and training MDW users to critically assess machine‐generated advice (World Health Organization 2023 ).

Practical approaches include community‐based participatory research workshops held on MDWs’ rest days at accessible venues (Israel et al. 2010 ), focus groups organized by language and country of origin to capture diverse perspectives, iterative prototype testing with real users to refine usability, and standing advisory panels that keep MDW voices central even after initial development ends.

Trained at the intersection of clinical care and information systems, they can ensure that chatbots and decision‐support tools use plain language consistent with health literacy principles, incorporate appropriate clinical safeguards, and maintain transparent privacy controls (Booth et al. 2021 ).

unlisted_practices: Require human review of AI health recommendations.
Build clear pathways for chatbot users to reach human providers.
Disclose to users that they are interacting with AI rather than a human and explain the limits of machine-generated advice.
Conduct privacy impact assessments for AI tools serving vulnerable migrant workers.
Specify data collection, storage, retention, and deletion rights in AI data governance frameworks.
Ensure critical medical advice from AI or machine translation is validated by bilingual healthcare professionals.
Conduct regular accuracy audits of AI health outputs against clinical guidelines.
Ensure AI in health augments rather than replaces human judgment.
Subsidize internet access, devices, and digital skills training so AI tools reach digitally excluded populations.
